content.label: The air was never the problem
content.lead: Dense ground fog does not reach the sky at all. The assumption was that the sky is checked too coarsely; it is not.

blocks.alt: how far the sky's dimming lands from the right answer

blocks.text: How far the sky's dimming lands from the truth, 0 being perfect — same sky, same coarseness, fog the only difference, 440 times worse.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.text: The fog layer is a hundred metres thick and the sky is checked in kilometre strides, so the render steps clean over it.

content.label: The exact fog, checked
content.lead: Measured against a brute-force answer computed a completely different way — 480 situations per fog type.

blocks.label: Teeth
blocks.text: Deliberately breaking one sign in the formula throws the answer 100% off and the check goes red.

blocks.label: The literature agrees
blocks.text: The dimming half of this formula is published games work from 2006, and nobody fixes a thin layer by spreading samples.

content.label: Every light the same
content.lead: You are right twice: there is no sunbeam, and there is no sun and moon — one kind of body, one set of rules.

blocks.label: I had this wrong
blocks.text: I told you the moon casts no shadows anywhere. It does — the scene already hands the shadows to whichever body is lighting it, and that crosses over at dusk.

rows: Fixed. Whichever body is lighting the scene throws the beams; at dusk, when both are up, the brighter one does
Nothing left to build in the fog — they just have to be handed to it, and that waits on sorting the scene's lights
Same, plus they emit nothing anywhere yet

blocks.label: Now built
blocks.text: The fog no longer knows which light is which. Proven by deliberately putting the privilege back: the same light then gave two different answers depending on where it sat in the list.
The fix is to stop the fog knowing which body is which: one list, each entry carrying its own shadow, so a beam is simply what a blocked glow looks like.

blocks.label: So there is no "add the lamps later"
blocks.text: Fog is handed the lights and treats them all the same. A source that did not exist when it was built still works — it just turns up in the list.

columns: Swept the whole game for it
rows: Places one body can do something the other cannot
Places the code calls it the sun when it means either
A shape that contradicts itself in one file
Things only one body can do that may be correct

blocks.label: Why names count
blocks.text: The naming is what made me report the moon as shadowless — a name that misleads its own reader is as real a fault as a wrong number.

blocks.label: The test earned its keep
blocks.text: It caught a lamp being placed about a metre from where it actually is, which would have made every lamp glow the wrong brightness. Fixed the same day.

content.label: What the wiring buys
content.lead: Today the sky's fog is worked out once from a fixed point 1.5 m above the ground and reused for everything.

rows: Drive up out of the fog and see clear sky
Fog in car paint matches the fog you see

blocks.text: Smaller than the plan assumed: ten things read the fog, but nine read it from two shared places, so the change lands in three.

blocks.label: Flat ground
blocks.text: The exact answer describes a flat fog layer on flat ground; a line of sight skimming the horizon is held at a shallow angle rather than curving with the planet.
Every such line of sight is already fully fogged, so the difference is invisible — but it is an approximation and it is written down as one.

decisions.title: Build the exact fog first; re-measure; spread samples only if something is left over
decisions.why: Reverses the plan's stated order, where sample-spreading jumped the queue, and folds a third planned fix in for free. Approved 12 Aug.

decisions.title: The sample-spreading step is paused, not deleted
decisions.why: Its background reading is filed. If the re-measure shows anything left over, it is ready to build immediately.

decisions.title: How the exact fog combines with the air's own dimming over long distances is mine to design
decisions.why: The fog answer is exact for fog alone; the two have to be woven together along the same line of sight. This is the one genuinely unsolved piece.

decisions.title: There is no sunbeam feature — every light interacts with fog and air identically
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug and binding on everything downstream: no light may be shadowed in the fog while another is not, and a beam is not a feature, it is what a blocked glow looks like.

decisions.title: The fog's body privilege and the trackside lamps now have owners in the plan
decisions.why: Was written as 'the moon has no shadows'. It has them — the gap is that the fog asks the sun's slot regardless of which body is lighting the scene.

decisions.title: There is no sun and no moon — one kind of body, the same rules for everything
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug. Which body it is may be data — its disc, its phase, its colour — never a rule that gives one of them something the other cannot have.

decisions.title: The job is one way in for light, not a fix per kind of light
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug. Fog is handed the lights and applies one physics to all of them, so a source built later works by turning up — there is no separate job to add it.

decisions.title: Nothing places a celestial body by hand; the sky obeys the time and the coordinates
decisions.why: Ruled 12 Aug. A body's position is a result of when and where you are, never something you set. The hand-set sun and the switch that reaches it are deleted, so a scene, a test or a preset states a time and a place instead.

next.if_nothing: I finish the one way in for light, wire the exact fog to everything that reads it, and come back with pictures.
